codes.name: target-unsupported
codes.title: unsupported build target
codes.summary: The target triple names a platform Mesh cannot compile or link for, or an artifact kind that the target does not support.
codes.repair: Pass `--target` a supported triple, a Unix-like one (macOS, iOS, Linux, Android, or a BSD) or a Windows MSVC one, or omit it to build for the host. Build an executable or a `cdylib` where the target has no `staticlib` support.

codes.name: linker-not-found
codes.title: linker not found
codes.summary: The C compiler, linker, or archiver the target links with could not be found or started.
codes.repair: Install the tool the message names and put it on `PATH`: a C compiler (`cc`) on Unix-like targets, `clang` from LLVM 21 for Windows MSVC (or set `LLVM_SYS_211_PREFIX` to that LLVM), or the Android NDK with `ANDROID_NDK_HOME` set.

codes.name: link-failed
codes.title: linking failed
codes.summary: The linker or archiver ran and reported a failure; its output is in the notes.
codes.repair: Fix what the linker output in the notes names: supply a missing native library or archive, and rebuild the Mesh runtime for the same target when its symbols are missing.

codes.name: runtime-library-missing
codes.title: runtime library missing
codes.summary: The Mesh runtime static library for the target was not found, or `MESH_RT_LIB_PATH` or `MESH_TEST_RT_LIB_PATH` does not name one.
codes.repair: Reinstall Mesh so the `lib` directory beside `meshc` holds the runtime, or in a source checkout run `cargo build -p mesh-rt` (`-p mesh-test-rt` for `meshc test`, with `--target` for another target). Point `MESH_RT_LIB_PATH` at the library file itself, or unset it.

codes.name: output-unwritable
codes.title: cannot write build output
codes.summary: The object file, LLVM IR, executable, or library could not be written at its output path.
codes.repair: Create the output directory, or pass `--output` a path in a writable directory where no directory of the same name exists.

codes.name: artifact-entry-missing
codes.title: artifact has no entry point
codes.summary: An executable build found no `fn main()` in the entry module, or a `staticlib` or `cdylib` build found no `@export` function for a host to call.
codes.repair: Define `fn main()` in the entrypoint to build an executable, or mark a public function `@export("symbol")` to build a library, or pass `--artifact` the kind of artifact the program provides.

codes.name: uncategorized
codes.title: uncategorized failure
codes.summary: A failure on a path that has no catalog code yet.
codes.repair: Fix what the message names. If the message does not say enough to act on, report it with the command that produced it.

codes.name: cluster-declaration-invalid
codes.title: invalid `@cluster` declaration
codes.summary: A `@cluster` decorator is on a private function, on a name with several public definitions, or on a target already declared as clustered work.
codes.repair: Put `@cluster` on exactly one `pub fn` per name: make the function public, give overloaded entrypoints distinct names, and remove any second decorator for the same target.

codes.name: type-mismatch
codes.title: type mismatch
codes.summary: A value's type differs from the type its position requires.
codes.repair: Convert the value (`Int.to_float(...)`, `Some(...)`, `Ok(...)`), change it, or change the annotation so both sides name one type.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let n :: Int = "one"
  println("#{n}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let n :: Int = 1
  println("#{n}")
end

codes.name: infinite-type
codes.title: infinite type
codes.summary: Inference needs a type that contains itself, as when a function is applied to itself.
codes.repair: Stop passing the value to itself or storing it inside itself. For recursive data, define a struct or sum type that refers to itself by name.

codes.name: arity-mismatch
codes.title: wrong number of arguments
codes.summary: A call passes more or fewer arguments than the function takes, or a closure of several parameters is given where a function of one tuple is expected.
codes.repair: Pass exactly the arguments the function declares; a value piped with `|>` counts as the first. To take a tuple argument apart, put its pattern in parentheses: `fn ((a, b)) -> ... end`.

example.bad:
fn add(a :: Int, b :: Int) -> Int = a + b

fn main() do
  println("#{add(1)}")
end
example.fixed:
fn add(a :: Int, b :: Int) -> Int = a + b

fn main() do
  println("#{add(1, 2)}")
end

codes.name: unbound-variable
codes.title: undefined variable
codes.summary: A name is used where nothing of that name is defined, imported, or in scope.
codes.repair: Define the name before this use, import the module that defines it, or correct the spelling to a name in scope.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let count = 1
  println("#{cuont}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let count = 1
  println("#{count}")
end

codes.name: not-a-function
codes.title: call of a non-function
codes.summary: A value that is not a function is called with parentheses.
codes.repair: Remove the parentheses to use the value itself, or call the function the value was meant to be.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let n = 1
  println("#{n()}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let n = 1
  println("#{n}")
end

codes.name: trait-not-satisfied
codes.title: interface not implemented
codes.summary: A type is used where an interface it does not implement is required, such as interpolating a struct that does not implement `Display`.
codes.repair: Add the interface to the type's `deriving(...)` list, or write `impl Interface for Type do ... end`.

example.bad:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end deriving(Eq)

fn main() do
  let p = Point { x: 1 }
  println("#{p}")
end
example.fixed:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end deriving(Eq, Display)

fn main() do
  let p = Point { x: 1 }
  println("#{p}")
end

codes.name: missing-trait-method
codes.title: missing interface method
codes.summary: An `impl` block leaves out a method its interface declares without a default body.
codes.repair: Add the missing `fn` to the `impl` block, with the signature the interface declares.

example.bad:
interface Shape do
  fn area(self) -> Int
end

struct Square do
  side :: Int
end

impl Shape for Square do
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
interface Shape do
  fn area(self) -> Int
end

struct Square do
  side :: Int
end

impl Shape for Square do
  fn area(self) -> Int do
    self.side * self.side
  end
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: trait-method-signature-mismatch
codes.title: impl method signature differs from its interface
codes.summary: A method in an `impl` block has other parameter or return types than its interface declares.
codes.repair: Change the method's parameter and return types to the ones the interface declares.

example.bad:
interface Shape do
  fn area(self) -> Int
end

struct Square do
  side :: Int
end

impl Shape for Square do
  fn area(self) -> String do
    "big"
  end
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
interface Shape do
  fn area(self) -> Int
end

struct Square do
  side :: Int
end

impl Shape for Square do
  fn area(self) -> Int do
    self.side * self.side
  end
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: invalid-field
codes.title: missing or unknown field
codes.summary: A struct literal leaves out a field or names one the struct does not have, or a field is read from a type without it.
codes.repair: Give every field the struct declares exactly once, and use only field names from the struct's definition.

example.bad:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
  y :: Int
end

fn main() do
  let p = Point { x: 1 }
  println("#{p.x}")
end
example.fixed:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
  y :: Int
end

fn main() do
  let p = Point { x: 1, y: 2 }
  println("#{p.x}")
end

codes.name: unknown-variant
codes.title: unknown variant
codes.summary: A pattern names a constructor that no sum type in scope defines.
codes.repair: Correct the spelling to a variant of the matched type, or import the module that defines the type. To split a list in a pattern, write `head :: tail` with a lowercase tail.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let n = case Some(1) do
    Some(v) -> v
    Nothing -> 0
  end
  println("#{n}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let n = case Some(1) do
    Some(v) -> v
    None -> 0
  end
  println("#{n}")
end

codes.name: or-pattern-binding-mismatch
codes.title: or-pattern alternatives bind different names
codes.summary: The alternatives of a `|` pattern bind different sets of variables, so the arm body cannot rely on any of them.
codes.repair: Bind the same names in every alternative, or split the alternatives into separate arms. A list's tail is written `head :: tail`, not `[head | tail]`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let n = case Some(1) do
    Some(a) | None -> 0
  end
  println("#{n}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let n = case Some(1) do
    Some(_) | None -> 0
  end
  println("#{n}")
end

codes.name: non-exhaustive-match
codes.title: non-exhaustive match
codes.summary: A `case` has no arm for some values of the matched type.
codes.repair: Add an arm for each missing pattern the diagnostic lists, or a final `_` arm for an intentional default.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let n = case Some(1) do
    Some(v) -> v
  end
  println("#{n}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let n = case Some(1) do
    Some(v) -> v
    None -> 0
  end
  println("#{n}")
end

codes.name: message-type-mismatch
codes.title: message type mismatch
codes.summary: A message sent to a typed `Pid<M>` is not of type `M`.
codes.repair: Send a value of the pid's message type, or change the actor's message type to one that includes this message.

example.bad:
actor counter(total :: Int) do
  receive do
    n -> counter(total + n)
  end
end

fn main() do
  let pid :: Pid<Int> = spawn(counter, 0)
  send(pid, "five")
end
example.fixed:
actor counter(total :: Int) do
  receive do
    n -> counter(total + n)
  end
end

fn main() do
  let pid :: Pid<Int> = spawn(counter, 0)
  send(pid, 5)
end

codes.name: self-outside-actor
codes.title: `self()` outside an actor
codes.summary: `self()` names the running actor, and it is called where no actor is running.
codes.repair: Move the `self()` call into an `actor` body, or pass the pid it should name in as an argument.

codes.name: spawn-non-function
codes.title: spawn of a non-function
codes.summary: `spawn` is given a value that is not an actor.
codes.repair: Pass the actor to start as the first argument, followed by its arguments: `spawn(worker, arg)`.

example.fixed:
actor worker() do
  println("started")
end

fn main() do
  let _ = spawn(worker)
end

codes.name: receive-outside-actor
codes.title: `receive` outside an actor
codes.summary: A `receive` block appears outside an actor, where there is no mailbox to read.
codes.repair: Move the `receive` block into an `actor name(...) do ... end` body.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  receive do
    _ -> println("got one")
  end
end
example.fixed:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    _ -> println("got one")
  end
end

fn main() do
  let _ = spawn(worker)
end

codes.name: invalid-child-start
codes.title: child start function does not return a pid
codes.summary: A supervisor child's `start` function returns something other than the `Pid` of the process it spawns.
codes.repair: Make `start` return the result of `spawn`, as `start: fn -> spawn(worker, arg) end`.

example.bad:
actor worker() do
  nil
end

supervisor Workers do
  strategy: one_for_one
  child worker do
    start: fn -> 42 end
  end
end
example.fixed:
actor worker() do
  nil
end

supervisor Workers do
  strategy: one_for_one
  child worker do
    start: fn -> spawn(worker) end
  end
end

codes.name: unknown-supervision-strategy
codes.title: unknown supervision strategy
codes.summary: A supervisor's `strategy` is not one Mesh supports.
codes.repair: Set `strategy:` to `one_for_one`, `one_for_all`, `rest_for_one`, or `simple_one_for_one`.

example.bad:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    _ -> println("done")
  end
end

supervisor WorkerSup do
  strategy: one_for_none

  child w do
    start: fn -> spawn(worker) end
    restart: transient
    shutdown: 1_000
  end
end

fn main() do
  let _ = spawn(WorkerSup)
end
example.fixed:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    _ -> println("done")
  end
end

supervisor WorkerSup do
  strategy: one_for_one

  child w do
    start: fn -> spawn(worker) end
    restart: transient
    shutdown: 1_000
  end
end

fn main() do
  let _ = spawn(WorkerSup)
end

codes.name: invalid-restart-type
codes.title: invalid restart type
codes.summary: A child spec's `restart` is not a restart type Mesh supports.
codes.repair: Set `restart:` to `permanent`, `transient`, or `temporary`.

example.bad:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    _ -> println("done")
  end
end

supervisor WorkerSup do
  strategy: one_for_one

  child w do
    start: fn -> spawn(worker) end
    restart: always
    shutdown: 1_000
  end
end

fn main() do
  let _ = spawn(WorkerSup)
end
example.fixed:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    _ -> println("done")
  end
end

supervisor WorkerSup do
  strategy: one_for_one

  child w do
    start: fn -> spawn(worker) end
    restart: transient
    shutdown: 1_000
  end
end

fn main() do
  let _ = spawn(WorkerSup)
end

codes.name: invalid-shutdown-value
codes.title: invalid shutdown value
codes.summary: A child spec's `shutdown` is neither a positive number of milliseconds nor `brutal_kill`.
codes.repair: Set `shutdown:` to a positive integer of milliseconds, such as `1_000`, or to `brutal_kill`.

example.bad:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    _ -> println("done")
  end
end

supervisor WorkerSup do
  strategy: one_for_one

  child w do
    start: fn -> spawn(worker) end
    restart: transient
    shutdown: forever
  end
end

fn main() do
  let _ = spawn(WorkerSup)
end
example.fixed:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    _ -> println("done")
  end
end

supervisor WorkerSup do
  strategy: one_for_one

  child w do
    start: fn -> spawn(worker) end
    restart: transient
    shutdown: 1_000
  end
end

fn main() do
  let _ = spawn(WorkerSup)
end

codes.name: catch-all-not-last
codes.title: catch-all clause before other clauses
codes.summary: A clause that matches every argument comes before other clauses of the same function, so they never run.
codes.repair: Move the catch-all clause after every more specific clause of the function.

example.bad:
fn label(n) = n
fn label(0) = 1
example.fixed:
fn label(0) = 1
fn label(n) = n

codes.name: non-consecutive-clauses
codes.title: function clauses are not consecutive
codes.summary: Clauses of one function name and arity are separated by other definitions.
codes.repair: Move every clause of the function together, one after another, or rename the later definition.

example.bad:
fn label(n) = "any"

fn main() do
  println(label(1))
end

fn label(n) = "other"
example.fixed:
fn label(n) = "any"

fn main() do
  println(label(1))
end

fn other_label(n) = "other"

codes.name: duplicate-impl
codes.title: duplicate impl
codes.summary: Two `impl` blocks implement the same interface for the same type.
codes.repair: Remove one of the `impl` blocks, or merge their methods into one.

example.bad:
interface Named do
  fn name(self) -> String
end

struct User do
  id :: Int
end

impl Named for User do
  fn name(self) -> String do
    "user"
  end
end

impl Named for User do
  fn name(self) -> String do
    "person"
  end
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
interface Named do
  fn name(self) -> String
end

struct User do
  id :: Int
end

impl Named for User do
  fn name(self) -> String do
    "user"
  end
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: ambiguous-method
codes.title: ambiguous method
codes.summary: Several interfaces implemented for the receiver's type provide a method of the called name.
codes.repair: Call the method through the interface you mean, as `Interface.method(value)`.

example.bad:
interface A do
  fn label(self) -> Int
end

interface B do
  fn label(self) -> Int
end

struct Item do
  n :: Int
end

impl A for Item do
  fn label(self) -> Int = self.n
end

impl B for Item do
  fn label(self) -> Int = self.n + 1
end

fn main() = Item { n: 0 }.label()
example.fixed:
interface A do
  fn label(self) -> Int
end

interface B do
  fn label(self) -> Int
end

struct Item do
  n :: Int
end

impl A for Item do
  fn label(self) -> Int = self.n
end

impl B for Item do
  fn label(self) -> Int = self.n + 1
end

fn main() = A.label(Item { n: 0 })

codes.name: unsupported-derive
codes.title: interface cannot be derived
codes.summary: A `deriving(...)` list names an interface that cannot be derived for this kind of type.
codes.repair: Derive only Eq, Ord, Display, Debug, Hash, Json, Row, or Schema on a struct, and the same but Row and Schema on a sum type. Write an `impl` for any other interface.

example.bad:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end deriving(Add)

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end deriving(Eq)

fn main() do
end

codes.name: missing-derive-prerequisite
codes.title: derived interface needs another
codes.summary: A derived interface depends on another that the `deriving` list leaves out, such as `Ord` without `Eq`.
codes.repair: Add the required interface to the same `deriving(...)` list.

example.bad:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end deriving(Ord)

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end deriving(Eq, Ord)

fn main() do
end

codes.name: no-such-method
codes.title: no such method
codes.summary: A method is called on a type that neither defines it nor implements an interface that provides it.
codes.repair: Correct the method name, call the module function it stands for as `Module.function(value)`, or implement an interface that provides the method.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let n = 1
  println(n.shout())
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let n = 1
  println(n.to_string())
end

codes.name: module-not-found
codes.title: module not found
codes.summary: An `import` names a module that is neither in the project nor in the standard library.
codes.repair: Correct the module path, which follows the file path (`geo/points.mpl` is `Geo.Points`), or create the module's file.

example.bad:
import Maths

module Math do
  pub fn count() = 1
end
example.fixed:
import Math

module Math do
  pub fn count() = 1
end

codes.name: break-outside-loop
codes.title: `break` outside a loop
codes.summary: `break` appears where no `while` or `for` loop encloses it.
codes.repair: Move the `break` into a loop body, or leave the function with `return` instead.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  break
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  while true do
    break
  end
end

codes.name: continue-outside-loop
codes.title: `continue` outside a loop
codes.summary: `continue` appears where no `while` or `for` loop encloses it.
codes.repair: Move the `continue` into a loop body, or remove it.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  continue
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  while false do
    continue
  end
end

codes.name: import-name-not-found
codes.title: imported name not exported
codes.summary: An import names something its module does not define.
codes.repair: Correct the name to one the module exports (the diagnostic lists them), or define it in the module with `pub`.

example.bad:
from Math import coun

module Math do
  pub fn count() = 1
end
example.fixed:
from Math import count

module Math do
  pub fn count() = 1
end

codes.name: private-item
codes.title: private item imported
codes.summary: An import names a definition its module does not mark `pub`.
codes.repair: Add `pub` to the definition in its module, or stop importing it.

example.bad:
from Math import count

module Math do
  fn count() = 1
end
example.fixed:
from Math import count

module Math do
  pub fn count() = 1
end

codes.name: try-incompatible-return
codes.title: `?` in a function that cannot return its failure
codes.summary: `?` returns early with the operand's `Err` or `None`, and the enclosing function's return type cannot hold it.
codes.repair: For a `Result` operand, make the function return a `Result` whose error type matches or has a `From` conversion; for an `Option` operand, return an `Option`. Otherwise handle the value with `case` instead of `?`.

example.bad:
fn half(n :: Int) -> Option<Int> do
  if n % 2 == 0 do
    Some(n / 2)
  else
    None
  end
end

fn quarter(n :: Int) -> Int do
  let h = half(n)?
  h / 2
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
fn half(n :: Int) -> Option<Int> do
  if n % 2 == 0 do
    Some(n / 2)
  else
    None
  end
end

fn quarter(n :: Int) -> Option<Int> do
  let h = half(n)?
  half(h)
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: try-on-non-result
codes.title: `?` on a value that is not a Result or Option
codes.summary: `?` unwraps only `Result` and `Option` values, and its operand is neither.
codes.repair: Remove the `?`, or apply it to an expression that returns a `Result` or an `Option`.

example.bad:
fn double(n :: Int) -> Int = n * 2

fn quadruple(n :: Int) -> Option<Int> do
  let d = double(n)?
  Some(d * 2)
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
fn double(n :: Int) -> Int = n * 2

fn quadruple(n :: Int) -> Option<Int> do
  let d = double(n)
  Some(d * 2)
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: non-serializable-field
codes.title: field cannot be encoded as JSON
codes.summary: A type deriving `Json` has a field whose type has no JSON form.
codes.repair: Add `deriving(Json)` to the field's type, or change the field to a JSON type: Int, Float, Bool, String, a tuple, Option, List, or a Map with String keys.

example.bad:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end

struct Shape do
  origin :: Point
end deriving(Json)

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end deriving(Json)

struct Shape do
  origin :: Point
end deriving(Json)

fn main() do
end

codes.name: non-mappable-field
codes.title: field cannot be read from a database row
codes.summary: A struct deriving `Row` has a field of a type a database column cannot hold.
codes.repair: Change the field to Int, Float, Bool, String, or an Option of one of them, or remove `Row` from the `deriving` list.

example.bad:
struct User do
  tags :: List<String>
end deriving(Row)

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
struct User do
  tags :: String
end deriving(Row)

fn main() do
end

codes.name: missing-associated-type
codes.title: missing associated type
codes.summary: An `impl` block leaves out an associated type its interface declares.
codes.repair: Add `type Name = ConcreteType` to the `impl` block for each associated type the interface declares.

example.bad:
interface Container do
  type Item
  fn first(self) -> Self.Item
end

struct IntBox do
  value :: Int
end

impl Container for IntBox do
  fn first(self) -> Int do
    self.value
  end
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
interface Container do
  type Item
  fn first(self) -> Self.Item
end

struct IntBox do
  value :: Int
end

impl Container for IntBox do
  type Item = Int
  fn first(self) -> Int do
    self.value
  end
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: extra-associated-type
codes.title: associated type the interface does not declare
codes.summary: An `impl` block binds an associated type its interface does not declare.
codes.repair: Remove the `type` binding from the `impl` block, or declare it in the interface with `type Name`.

example.bad:
interface Labeled do
  fn label(self) -> String
end

struct IntBox do
  value :: Int
end

impl Labeled for IntBox do
  type Item = Int
  fn label(self) -> String do
    "box"
  end
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
interface Labeled do
  fn label(self) -> String
end

struct IntBox do
  value :: Int
end

impl Labeled for IntBox do
  fn label(self) -> String do
    "box"
  end
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: unresolved-associated-type
codes.title: unresolved associated type
codes.summary: `Self.Name` refers to an associated type that no interface in scope declares.
codes.repair: Declare the associated type in the interface with `type Name`, and bind it in each `impl` with `type Name = ConcreteType`.

example.bad:
interface Container do
  fn first(self) -> Self.Item
end
example.fixed:
interface Container do
  type Item
  fn first(self) -> Self.Item
end

codes.name: slot-pipe-out-of-range
codes.title: slot pipe position out of range
codes.summary: `|N>` passes the piped value as argument N, and the function takes fewer than N arguments.
codes.repair: Use a position from 2 up to the function's arity, or `|>` to pass the value as the first argument.

example.bad:
fn add(a :: Int, b :: Int) -> Int = a + b

fn main() do
  let n = 1 |3> add(2)
  println("#{n}")
end
example.fixed:
fn add(a :: Int, b :: Int) -> Int = a + b

fn main() do
  let n = 1 |2> add(2)
  println("#{n}")
end

codes.name: undefined-alias-target
codes.title: type alias names an undefined type
codes.summary: A `type Name = Target` alias names a target type that does not exist.
codes.repair: Correct the target's spelling, import it, or define it as a struct, sum type, or alias.

example.bad:
type Count = Integer

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
type Count = Int

fn main() do
end

codes.name: manual-continuity-promotion
codes.title: manual continuity promotion is disabled
codes.summary: `Continuity.promote()` is no longer part of Mesh; failover between nodes is automatic.
codes.repair: Remove the `Continuity.promote()` call. Read authority state with `Continuity.authority_status()` where the program needs it.

example.bad: fn main() = Continuity.promote()
example.fixed: fn main() = Continuity.authority_status()

codes.name: clustered-route-invalid-arguments
codes.title: invalid `HTTP.clustered` arguments
codes.summary: `HTTP.clustered(...)` received arguments other than an optional replication count and a handler reference.
codes.repair: Write `HTTP.clustered(handler)` or `HTTP.clustered(count, handler)`, where `handler` names a public top-level route handler.

example.bad:
pub fn handle(req :: Request) -> Response = HTTP.response(200, "ok")

fn routes() = HTTP.on_get(HTTP.router(), "/", HTTP.clustered(0, handle))
example.fixed:
pub fn handle(req :: Request) -> Response = HTTP.response(200, "ok")

fn routes() = HTTP.on_get(HTTP.router(), "/", HTTP.clustered(handle))

codes.name: clustered-route-private-handler
codes.title: clustered route handler is private
codes.summary: `HTTP.clustered(...)` wraps a handler that is not `pub`, so other nodes cannot run it.
codes.repair: Add `pub` to the handler's definition, or remove the `HTTP.clustered(...)` wrapper.

example.bad:
fn handle(req :: Request) -> Response = HTTP.response(200, "ok")

fn routes() = HTTP.on_get(HTTP.router(), "/", HTTP.clustered(handle))
example.fixed:
pub fn handle(req :: Request) -> Response = HTTP.response(200, "ok")

fn routes() = HTTP.on_get(HTTP.router(), "/", HTTP.clustered(handle))

codes.name: clustered-route-misplaced
codes.title: `HTTP.clustered` outside a route handler position
codes.summary: `HTTP.clustered(...)` appears somewhere other than the handler argument of `HTTP.route(...)` or `HTTP.on_*(...)`.
codes.repair: Pass `HTTP.clustered(handler)` directly as the handler argument of `HTTP.route(...)` or `HTTP.on_*(...)`.

example.bad:
pub fn handle(req :: Request) -> Response = HTTP.response(200, "ok")

fn routes() = HTTP.clustered(handle)
example.fixed:
pub fn handle(req :: Request) -> Response = HTTP.response(200, "ok")

fn routes() = HTTP.on_get(HTTP.router(), "/", HTTP.clustered(handle))

codes.name: clustered-route-conflicting-count
codes.title: conflicting clustered route replication counts
codes.summary: One clustered route handler is wrapped with different replication counts in different places.
codes.repair: Use one replication count for the handler everywhere it is wrapped in `HTTP.clustered(...)`.

example.bad:
pub fn handle(req :: Request) -> Response = HTTP.response(200, "ok")

fn routes() do
  let router = HTTP.on_get(HTTP.router(), "/a", HTTP.clustered(2, handle))
  HTTP.on_get(router, "/b", HTTP.clustered(3, handle))
end
example.fixed:
pub fn handle(req :: Request) -> Response = HTTP.response(200, "ok")

fn routes() do
  let router = HTTP.on_get(HTTP.router(), "/a", HTTP.clustered(2, handle))
  HTTP.on_get(router, "/b", HTTP.clustered(2, handle))
end

codes.name: clustered-route-origin-missing
codes.title: imported clustered handler has no defining module
codes.summary: A handler imported by bare name into `HTTP.clustered(...)` has lost the module that defines it, so its runtime name is unknown.
codes.repair: Import the handler's module and wrap the handler by its qualified name, as `HTTP.clustered(Module.handler)`.

codes.name: invalid-native-declaration
codes.title: invalid native declaration
codes.summary: In a native binding listed in `mesh.toml`, an `@native` function is private, generic, missing a type annotation, or names a symbol that is not a C identifier.
codes.repair: Declare it as a public, non-generic function with every parameter and the return type annotated, and a C identifier as its symbol.

example.bad:
@native("mesh_count")
fn count() -> Int
example.fixed:
@native("mesh_count")
pub fn count() -> Int

codes.name: resource-ownership-violation
codes.title: resource ownership violation
codes.summary: A resource is used after a move, moved while borrowed, or given more than one owner.
codes.repair: Use the resource before moving it. Pass it to a direct `borrow` parameter when the caller needs to keep ownership.

example.bad:
fn close(secret :: SecretBytes) do
  Secret.destroy(secret)
  Secret.destroy(secret)
end
example.fixed:
fn close(secret :: SecretBytes) do
  Secret.destroy(secret)
end

codes.name: invalid-let-pattern
codes.title: invalid destructuring pattern
codes.summary: A `let` pattern could fail to match, or uses a form `let` cannot bind.
codes.repair: Bind only lowercase names, `_`, tuples, and struct patterns in `let`; match a value that may not fit with `case`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let (1, b) = (1, 2)
  println("#{b}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let (_, b) = (1, 2)
  println("#{b}")
end

codes.name: invalid-export-declaration
codes.title: invalid export declaration
codes.summary: An `@export` function does not have the binary request and response signature library exports use.
codes.repair: Declare the export as `@export("c_symbol") pub fn name(request :: Bytes) -> Bytes!String`.

example.bad:
@export("mesh_echo")
fn echo(request :: Bytes) -> Bytes!String = Ok(request)
example.fixed:
@export("mesh_echo")
pub fn echo(request :: Bytes) -> Bytes!String = Ok(request)

codes.name: invalid-pass-through-arm
codes.title: arm without `->` whose pattern is not a value
codes.summary: A match arm with no `->` gives its pattern as its value, and this pattern cannot stand for one.
codes.repair: Write the arm's value after `->`, as `pattern -> value`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  case 1 do
    _
  end
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  case 1 do
    _ -> 1
  end
end

codes.name: duplicate-binding
codes.title: name bound twice in a pattern
codes.summary: One pattern binds the same name in two places.
codes.repair: Rename one of the bindings. To require the two values to be equal, compare them in a `when` guard.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let n = case (1, 2) do
    (a, a) -> a
  end
  println("#{n}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let n = case (1, 2) do
    (a, b) -> a + b
  end
  println("#{n}")
end

codes.name: duplicate-field
codes.title: field given twice
codes.summary: A struct literal or update gives the same field more than once.
codes.repair: Give each field one value, and remove the repeated one.

example.bad:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end

fn main() do
  let p = Point { x: 1, x: 2 }
  println("#{p.x}")
end
example.fixed:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end

fn main() do
  let p = Point { x: 1 }
  println("#{p.x}")
end

codes.name: not-a-struct
codes.title: struct syntax on a non-struct
codes.summary: A struct literal or a `%{value | field: new}` update is applied to something that is not a struct, or whose type is not known there.
codes.repair: Use struct literals and updates only on struct types, and annotate the value with its struct type when nothing else fixes it.

example.bad: fn main() = Int { n: 1 }
example.fixed:
struct Count do
  n :: Int
end

fn main() = Count { n: 1 }

codes.name: underivable-function-field
codes.title: derived interface over a function field
codes.summary: A derived interface would compare, hash, or show a field that holds a function.
codes.repair: Remove the interface from the `deriving` list, or write an `impl` that leaves the function field out.

example.bad:
struct Handler do
  run :: Fun(Int) -> Int
end deriving(Eq)

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
struct Handler do
  run :: Fun(Int) -> Int
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: duplicate-variant
codes.title: variant name used by two types
codes.summary: Two sum types in one module declare a variant of the same name, so the name could mean either.
codes.repair: Rename one of the variants, or move one of the sum types to its own module.

example.bad:
type Light do
  Red
  Green
end

type Alert do
  Red
  Calm
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
type Light do
  Red
  Green
end

type Alert do
  Critical
  Calm
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: cyclic-alias
codes.title: type alias refers to itself
codes.summary: A type alias expands into itself, directly or through other aliases, so its expansion never ends.
codes.repair: Point the alias at an existing type. For a recursive type, define a struct or sum type instead.

example.bad:
type Loop = Loop

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
type Loop = Int

fn main() do
end

codes.name: unbounded-type-parameter
codes.title: type parameter needs an interface bound
codes.summary: A generic function applies an operator to a type parameter that no bound says supports it.
codes.repair: Add `where T: Interface` to the function's signature, naming the interface the operator needs, such as `Add` for `+`.

example.bad:
fn double<T>(x :: T) -> T do
  x + x
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
fn double<T>(x :: T) -> T where T: Add do
  x + x
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: ambiguous-default
codes.title: ambiguous `default()`
codes.summary: A `default()` call appears where nothing fixes which type of value it builds.
codes.repair: Annotate the binding with the type to build, as `let x :: Int = default()`.

codes.name: ambiguous-impl-method
codes.title: ambiguous impl method
codes.summary: Several `impl`s provide the called method with different return or argument types, and nothing at the call picks one.
codes.repair: Annotate the result, or the argument, with one of the types the diagnostic lists.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let x = 5.into()
  println("#{x}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let x :: Float = 5.into()
  println("#{x}")
end

codes.name: ambiguous-static-method
codes.title: ambiguous static method
codes.summary: A static interface method, one without `self`, is called bare while several types provide it.
codes.repair: Call it on the type that should provide it, as `Type.method()`.

example.bad:
interface Versioned do
  fn version() -> Int
end

struct A do
  n :: Int
end

struct B do
  n :: Int
end

impl Versioned for A do
  fn version() -> Int = 1
end

impl Versioned for B do
  fn version() -> Int = 2
end

fn main() = version()
example.fixed:
interface Versioned do
  fn version() -> Int
end

struct A do
  n :: Int
end

struct B do
  n :: Int
end

impl Versioned for A do
  fn version() -> Int = 1
end

impl Versioned for B do
  fn version() -> Int = 2
end

fn main() = A.version()

codes.name: rigid-type-parameter
codes.title: generic function fixes its type parameter
codes.summary: A generic function's body treats a type parameter as one particular type, though callers may pass any type.
codes.repair: Replace the type parameter with that type in the signature, or keep the parameter's values opaque in the body.

example.bad:
fn same<T>(x :: T) -> Int = x

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
fn same<T>(x :: T) -> T = x

fn main() do
end

codes.name: duplicate-definition
codes.title: defined twice
codes.summary: A field, variant, parameter, or type of one name is defined twice in the same scope.
codes.repair: Rename or remove one of the two definitions.

example.bad:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
  x :: Int
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
  y :: Int
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: unknown-type
codes.title: unknown type
codes.summary: An annotation names a type that is not defined, imported, or built in.
codes.repair: Correct the spelling, define the type, or import the module that defines it.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let _n :: Integer = 1
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let _n :: Int = 1
end

codes.name: unknown-field-owner
codes.title: field read from a value of unknown type
codes.summary: A field is read from a value whose type nothing fixes, so the struct that owns the field is unknown.
codes.repair: Annotate the value with its struct type, such as a parameter `p :: Point`.

example.bad:
fn get_x(p) = p.x

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end

fn get_x(p :: Point) -> Int = p.x

fn main() do
end

codes.name: unknown-interface
codes.title: unknown interface
codes.summary: An `impl` names an interface that is not defined, imported, or built in.
codes.repair: Correct the spelling, declare the interface, or import the module that defines it.

example.bad:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end

impl Printable for Point do
  fn print(self) -> String do
    "point"
  end
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
interface Printable do
  fn print(self) -> String
end

struct Point do
  x :: Int
end

impl Printable for Point do
  fn print(self) -> String do
    "point"
  end
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: invalid-literal
codes.title: invalid numeric literal
codes.summary: A numeric literal is malformed or does not fit its type.
codes.repair: Write a value in range for its type, using only the digits and `_` separators its base allows.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let n = 99999999999999999999
  println("#{n}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let n = 9_999
  println("#{n}")
end

codes.name: invalid-concat
codes.title: concatenation of values that are not strings or lists
codes.summary: `<>` joins strings and `++` joins lists, and these operands are neither.
codes.repair: Convert the operands to strings first, as `"#{a}#{b}"`, or use the operator their type has, such as `+` for numbers.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let a = 1
  let b = 2
  println(a <> b)
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let a = 1
  let b = 2
  println("#{a}#{b}")
end

codes.name: no-such-module-function
codes.title: no such module function
codes.summary: `Module.name` names a function the module does not define.
codes.repair: Correct the name to a function the module defines; the diagnostic lists them.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  println(String.upper("hi"))
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  println(String.to_upper("hi"))
end

codes.name: overloaded-function-value
codes.title: function of several arities used as a value
codes.summary: A function defined at several arities is referenced without a call, so the reference names no single function.
codes.repair: Call it with the arguments of one arity, or wrap the arity you mean in a closure, as `fn a -> name(a) end`.

example.bad:
fn area(w :: Int) -> Int = w * w
fn area(w :: Int, h :: Int) -> Int = w * h

fn main() do
  let _f = area
end
example.fixed:
fn area(w :: Int) -> Int = w * w
fn area(w :: Int, h :: Int) -> Int = w * h

fn main() do
  let _f = fn w -> area(w) end
end

codes.name: generic-impl-target
codes.title: impl for a generic type
codes.summary: An `impl` is written for a type that takes type parameters, which Mesh does not support.
codes.repair: Implement the interface for a type without type parameters, such as a struct that holds the generic one at a concrete type.

example.bad:
interface Named do
  fn name(self) -> String
end

struct Box<T> do
  value :: T
end

impl Named for Box do
  fn name(self) -> String do
    "box"
  end
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
interface Named do
  fn name(self) -> String
end

struct IntBox do
  value :: Int
end

impl Named for IntBox do
  fn name(self) -> String do
    "box"
  end
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: assert-receive-outside-test
codes.title: `assert_receive` outside a test file
codes.summary: `assert_receive` is expanded only in test files that `meshc test` runs.
codes.repair: Move the assertion into a `.test.mpl` file, or write the `receive ... after TIMEOUT -> ...` block it stands for.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  assert_receive 42, 500
end
example.fixed:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    42 -> nil
    _ -> nil
  after 500 -> nil
  end
end

codes.name: indexing-unsupported
codes.title: indexing syntax is not supported
codes.summary: `value[index]` is used, and Mesh has no indexing syntax.
codes.repair: Use `List.get(list, index)`, `Map.get(map, key)`, or `Tuple.nth(tuple, index)`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let xs = [1, 2, 3]
  let _first = xs[0]
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let xs = [1, 2, 3]
  let _first = List.get(xs, 0)
end

codes.name: actor-message-type-unknown
codes.title: actor message type unknown
codes.summary: Nothing in the module tells which type of message an actor receives, because only untyped pids reach it.
codes.repair: Give the pid a message type where the actor is spawned, as `let pid :: Pid<Int> = spawn(worker)`.

example.bad:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    msg -> msg
  end
end
example.fixed:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    msg -> msg + 1
  end
end

codes.name: top-level-let
codes.title: `let` outside a function
codes.summary: A `let` appears at the top level of a module, which has no global bindings.
codes.repair: Move the binding into the function that uses it, or define a function of no arguments for it, as `fn limit() = 10`.

example.bad:
let limit = 10

fn main() do
  println("#{limit}")
end
example.fixed:
fn limit() = 10

fn main() do
  println("#{limit()}")
end

codes.name: module-not-imported
codes.title: module used without an import
codes.summary: Code calls a function of a project module that the file does not import.
codes.repair: Add `import Module` at the top of the file.

example.bad:
module Counters do
  pub fn count() = 1
end

fn main() = Counters.count()
example.fixed:
import Counters

module Counters do
  pub fn count() = 1
end

fn main() = Counters.count()

codes.name: untyped-method-parameter
codes.title: method parameter type unknown
codes.summary: A method parameter has no annotation and nothing in the method fixes its type; a method is compiled once, for the type it is implemented for.
codes.repair: Annotate the parameter with its type, as `param :: Type`.

example.bad:
interface Labeler do
  fn label(self, x) -> String
end

struct Item do
  n :: Int
end

impl Labeler for Item do
  fn label(self, x) -> String = "#{x}"
end
example.fixed:
interface Labeler do
  fn label(self, x) -> String
end

struct Item do
  n :: Int
end

impl Labeler for Item do
  fn label(self, x :: Int) -> String = "#{x}"
end

codes.name: type-not-value
codes.title: type used as a value
codes.summary: A type's name is used where a value is expected.
codes.repair: Build a value of the type (`Name { ... }` for a struct, a variant for a sum type), or call one of its functions, as `Name.function(...)`.

example.bad:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end

fn main() do
  let _p = Point
end
example.fixed:
struct Point do
  x :: Int
end

fn main() do
  let _p = Point { x: 1 }
end

codes.name: nested-definition
codes.title: definition inside a function
codes.summary: A definition such as `fn`, `struct`, or `import` appears inside a function body, where only `let` binds names.
codes.repair: Move the definition to the top level of the module. For a local function, bind a closure: `let name = fn x -> ... end`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  fn helper() = 1
end
example.fixed:
fn helper() = 1

fn main() do
end

codes.name: type-argument-count
codes.title: wrong number of type arguments
codes.summary: A generic type is named with another number of type arguments than it declares.
codes.repair: Pass exactly as many type arguments as the type declares, as `Option<Int>`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let _x :: Option<Int, String> = None
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let _x :: Option<Int> = None
end

codes.name: monitor-outside-actor
codes.title: monitor outside an actor
codes.summary: `Process.monitor` or `Node.monitor` is called outside an actor, so its message has no actor to go to.
codes.repair: Call `Process.monitor` or `Node.monitor` inside the actor body that should receive the message.

example.bad: fn main() = Node.monitor("node@localhost:9000", 1)
example.fixed:
actor watcher() do
  Node.monitor("node@localhost:9000", 1)
  receive do
    n -> n + 1
  end
end

codes.name: top-level-statement
codes.title: statement outside a function
codes.summary: An expression appears at the top level of a module, where nothing runs it.
codes.repair: Move the expression into `main` or into the function that should run it.

example.bad:
println("hi")

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  println("hi")
end

codes.name: method-return-unknown
codes.title: method return type unknown
codes.summary: A method an `impl` provides has a return type nothing fixes, so a call to it cannot be typed.
codes.repair: Annotate the method's return type in the `impl` or the interface, as `fn name(self) -> Type`.

example.fixed:
interface Maker do
  fn make(self) -> Int
end

struct Item do
  n :: Int
end

impl Maker for Item do
  fn make(self) -> Int = self.n
end

fn main() = Item { n: 0 }.make()

codes.name: spawn-computed
codes.title: spawn of a computed function
codes.summary: `spawn` is given a function computed at run time, and a process starts from a compiled entry that only a name gives.
codes.repair: Name the actor in the call, as `spawn(worker, arg)`. To choose one at run time, spawn each by name where it is chosen.

example.bad:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    msg -> msg + 1
  end
end

fn pick() = worker

fn main() = spawn(pick())
example.fixed:
actor worker() do
  receive do
    msg -> msg + 1
  end
end

fn pick() = worker

fn main() = spawn(worker)

codes.name: spawn-not-actor
codes.title: spawn of a function that is not an actor
codes.summary: `spawn` names a plain `fn`, and only an `actor` runs as a process of its own.
codes.repair: Define what runs in the new process as `actor name(...) do ... end` and spawn that, or call the function directly.

example.bad:
fn hello() do
  println("hi")
end

fn main() do
  let _ = spawn(hello)
end
example.fixed:
actor hello() do
  println("hi")
end

fn main() do
  let _ = spawn(hello)
end

codes.name: decode-type-unknown
codes.title: decoded type unknown
codes.summary: A generic type's `from_json` is called where nothing fixes its type arguments.
codes.repair: Annotate the result with the full type, as `let r :: Result<Box<Int>, String> = Box.from_json(text)`.

codes.name: underivable-field-type
codes.title: field type lacks the derived interface
codes.summary: A derived interface needs every field to implement it, and one field's type does not.
codes.repair: Derive or implement the interface for the field's type, or remove the interface from the `deriving` list.

example.bad:
struct Inner do
  x :: Int
end deriving(Display)

struct Outer do
  inner :: Inner
end deriving(Eq)

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
struct Inner do
  x :: Int
end deriving(Display, Eq)

struct Outer do
  inner :: Inner
end deriving(Eq)

fn main() do
end

codes.name: plaintext-violation
codes.title: plaintext leaves the program
codes.summary: A `Plaintext` value, or one holding it, reaches a way out of the program other than a seal, an `@display` export, or `declassify`.
codes.repair: Seal the value with `Crypto.aead_seal_plaintext`, `Crypto.hpke_seal_plaintext`, or `Plaintext.seal_for_storage`, export it through `@display`, or release it with `declassify(value, "reason")`. Transform it in place with `Plaintext.map`.

example.bad: fn show(text :: Plaintext<String>) = declassify(text, "")
example.fixed: fn show(text :: Plaintext<String>) = declassify(text, "explicit display")

codes.name: invalid-jobs-start
codes.title: invalid `Jobs.start` call
codes.summary: `Jobs.start` is used indirectly or given a handler the compiler cannot check.
codes.repair: Call `Jobs.start` directly, and pass a named function of type `fn(String) -> String` as its handler.

example.bad:
fn start(pool :: PoolHandle) do
  Jobs.start(pool, "{}", fn job -> job end)
end
example.fixed:
fn handle(job :: String) -> String = job

fn start(pool :: PoolHandle) do
  Jobs.start(pool, "{}", handle)
end

codes.name: invalid-nat-index
codes.title: invalid Nat index
codes.summary: A static `Nat` index is malformed: an index parameter is not of kind `Nat` or is not on a sum type, variant, or function; a literal does not fit in 64 bits; a type and a Nat index stand in each other's place; or an index escapes the case arm that binds it.
codes.repair: Declare each index parameter as `n :: Nat` on a sum type, variant, or function, and write each index from `Nat` literals, those parameters, and `Succ<...>`, with types only in type positions. Return a value whose type names no index bound inside a case arm.

example.bad:
fn count<n :: Int>() -> Int = 0

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
fn count<n :: Nat>() -> Int = 0

fn main() do
end

codes.name: invalid-indexed-type
codes.title: invalid indexed type
codes.summary: An indexed sum type, one of its constructors, or a function with index parameters breaks a rule of indexed types, or an indexed type is used without its arguments or matched by a constructor it cannot have.
codes.repair: Give each constructor of an indexed type a result `-> Family<...>` of its own family that keeps the type parameters and binds every constructor index; write the family with all its arguments; declare index parameters once, without trait bounds, on a function of one clause; derive nothing; and match its constructors in a direct `case` arm.

example.bad:
type Vec<T, n :: Nat> do
  Empty
  Push<k :: Nat>(T, Vec<T, k>) -> Vec<T, Succ<k>>
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
type Vec<T, n :: Nat> do
  Empty -> Vec<T, 0>
  Push<k :: Nat>(T, Vec<T, k>) -> Vec<T, Succ<k>>
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: reserved-proof-name
codes.title: `Proof` is a reserved type name
codes.summary: A struct, sum type, or type alias is named `Proof`, the name of the type of proof values.
codes.repair: Rename the type, for example to `Evidence`, and update its uses.

example.bad:
struct Proof do
  value :: Int
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
struct Evidence do
  value :: Int
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: missing-embedded-proof
codes.title: exported theorem without a proof
codes.summary: A `pub theorem` in a `logic do` block has no `proof` of the same name in the module, so there is no proof value to export.
codes.repair: Write `proof name do ... end` for the theorem in a `logic do` block of the same module, or remove `pub` to keep the theorem out of Mesh code.

example.bad:
logic do
  pub theorem two() do 2 == 2 end
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
logic do
  pub theorem two() do 2 == 2 end
  proof two do refl end
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: duplicate-proof-value
codes.title: proof value defined twice
codes.summary: Two `pub theorem`s in one module's `logic do` blocks have the same name, so the name would stand for two proof values.
codes.repair: Rename one of the theorems and its `proof`, and update the calls that use it.

example.bad:
logic do
  pub theorem two() do 2 == 2 end
  proof two do refl end
  pub theorem two() do 1 + 1 == 2 end
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
logic do
  pub theorem two() do 2 == 2 end
  proof two do refl end
  pub theorem sum() do 1 + 1 == 2 end
  proof sum do refl end
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: invalid-proposition
codes.title: invalid proposition
codes.summary: A proposition has no Mesh proof type: an exported theorem or a `Proof<...>` annotation states something other than a known `Prop` predicate of Nat arguments or a `NatEq` of two Nat terms, or a theorem that takes parameters is used without them.
codes.repair: State the proposition as a predicate declared `-> Prop` in a `logic do` block, applied to Nat literals, `Nat.succ`, or index parameters, or as an equality of Nat terms (`Proof<NatEq<a, b>>` in a type). Call a theorem with parameters as `name(indices..., proofs...)`.

example.bad:
fn accept(evidence :: Proof<NatEq<2>>) -> Int = 2

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
fn accept(evidence :: Proof<NatEq<2, 2>>) -> Int = 2

fn main() do
end

codes.name: resource-crosses-boundary
codes.title: resource crosses an ownership boundary
codes.summary: A resource reaches an operation that cannot preserve its single owner, such as an actor message, job, collection, or serialization.
codes.repair: Keep the resource in an ownership-aware scope and pass an unrestricted value instead, such as an ID or the data the resource represents.

example.bad:
resource struct Handle do
  id :: Int
end

fn forward(pid :: Pid, handle :: Handle) = send(pid, handle)
example.fixed:
resource struct Handle do
  id :: Int
end

fn forward(pid :: Pid, handle :: Handle) = send(pid, handle.id)

codes.name: duplicate-type-across-modules
codes.title: type name shared by multiple modules
codes.summary: Two modules define the same struct, sum type, interface, actor, service, or supervisor name. These declarations share a project-wide namespace, even when private.
codes.repair: Rename all but one definition and update its uses, or keep one shared definition and import it where needed.

example.bad:
module A do
  struct State do
    count :: Int
  end
end

module B do
  struct State do
    name :: String
  end
end
example.fixed:
module A do
  struct State do
    count :: Int
  end
end

module B do
  struct NamedState do
    name :: String
  end
end

codes.name: duplicate-pub-fn-across-modules
codes.title: public function symbol shared by multiple modules
codes.summary: Two modules export a public function with the same compiler symbol. Calls could run only one of the definitions even when the import names the other module.
codes.repair: Rename all but one public function and update its callers, or make the other functions private if their callers are in the same module.

example.bad:
module A do
  pub fn count() do
    1
  end
end

module B do
  pub fn count() do
    2
  end
end
example.fixed:
module A do
  pub fn count() do
    1
  end
end

module B do
  pub fn total() do
    2
  end
end

codes.name: recursive-by-value-type
codes.title: struct holds itself by value
codes.summary: A struct holds itself by value, directly or through other structs, so a value of it would contain itself and could never be built.
codes.repair: Hold the recursive field through a type that ends the recursion: an `Option<...>` or a `List<...>` of the struct, or a sum type with a variant that does not hold it.

example.bad:
struct Node do
  next :: Node
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
struct Node do
  next :: Option<Node>
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: runtime-symbol-collision
codes.title: name already used by the runtime
codes.summary: A public function or a native binding takes a symbol that the Mesh runtime, the compiler, or another native binding already uses, so calls could reach the wrong code.
codes.repair: Rename the function, leaving names that start with `mesh_` to the runtime, and bind each native symbol once with one signature.

example.bad:
pub fn mesh_string_length(text :: String) -> Int = 0

fn main() do
  println("${mesh_string_length("abc")}")
end
example.fixed:
pub fn text_length(text :: String) -> Int = 0

fn main() do
  println("${text_length("abc")}")
end

codes.name: spawn-grouped-unsafe
codes.title: grouped actor may block its worker
codes.summary: An actor started with `spawn grouped`, or its `terminate` callback, can reach code the compiler cannot prove yields or returns without blocking the shared worker (a native or unaudited runtime call such as I/O, an indirect call, recursion that grows the stack, or a loop in a terminate callback), or `spawn grouped` starts a supervisor child.
codes.repair: Start the actor with plain `spawn`, or move the call the notes trace into an actor started with `spawn` and message it. Write recursion as a tail call, and keep loops out of terminate callbacks.

example.bad:
actor worker() do
  IO.eprintln("working")
end

fn main() do
  spawn grouped(worker)
end
example.fixed:
actor worker() do
  IO.eprintln("working")
end

fn main() do
  spawn(worker)
end

codes.name: node-spawn-argument
codes.title: `Node.spawn` cannot start this on another node
codes.summary: `Node.spawn` or `Node.spawn_link` is given a closure instead of a function defined at the top level, or an argument of a type that cannot cross the connection.
codes.repair: Name a top-level actor as the second argument, and pass it only `Int`, `Float`, `Bool`, `String`, `Pid`, or `()` arguments, encoding other data as a `String`.

example.fixed:
actor remote() do
  println("started")
end

actor spawner(host :: String) do
  let _ = Node.spawn(host, remote)
end

fn main() do
  let _ = spawn(spawner, "absent@127.0.0.1:1")
end

codes.name: export-symbol-collision
codes.title: exported symbol already taken
codes.summary: An `@export` C symbol is also another export's, a public Mesh function's, or the Mesh runtime's, so a host could not tell which one it calls.
codes.repair: Give each `@export` its own C symbol, prefixed with the library's name as in `@export("greeter_echo")`, that no public function or `mesh_` runtime symbol uses.

example.bad:
@export("mesh_println")
pub fn echo(request :: Bytes) -> Bytes ! String do
  Ok(request)
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
@export("greeter_echo")
pub fn echo(request :: Bytes) -> Bytes ! String do
  Ok(request)
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: internal-compiler-error
codes.title: internal compiler error
codes.summary: The compiler reached a state it should never reach; the program may well be valid.
codes.repair: Report it with the notes and the smallest program that reproduces it. Until it is fixed, rewrite the construct the notes name another way.

codes.name: internal-consistency-warning
codes.title: internal compiler consistency warning
codes.summary: During lowering, the compiler could not confirm the target trait method for a call that passed type checking.
codes.repair: Report the method name, receiver type, and a small program that reproduces the warning. Use an explicit function call if it resolves the intended method.

codes.name: deep-nesting
codes.title: control flow nested too deeply
codes.summary: An `if`, `case`, loop, `receive`, or closure is nested more than four levels deep in one function, counted from the function, handler, actor body, or top-level test block that holds it.
codes.repair: Move the construct the label points at into a function of its own and call it, return early from the enclosing function, or use `?` in place of a `case` that only passes an error on.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let n = 5
  if n > 0 do
    if n > 1 do
      if n > 2 do
        if n > 3 do
          if n > 4 do
            println("deep")
          end
        end
      end
    end
  end
end
example.fixed:
fn report(n :: Int) do
  if n > 4 do
    println("deep")
  end
end

fn main() do
  let n = 5
  if n > 0 do
    if n > 1 do
      if n > 2 do
        if n > 3 do
          report(n)
        end
      end
    end
  end
end

codes.name: collapsible-else-if
codes.title: `else` holding only an `if`
codes.summary: The whole body of an `else` is one `if` expression, which `else if` says one level shallower.
codes.repair: Join `else` and the `if` it holds into `else if ... do`, outdent that `if`'s branches one level, and delete the `end` that closed the `else`, so the inner `if`'s `end` closes the whole chain.

example.bad:
fn sign(n :: Int) -> String do
  if n > 0 do
    "positive"
  else
    if n < 0 do
      "negative"
    else
      "zero"
    end
  end
end

fn main() do
  println(sign(-1))
end
example.fixed:
fn sign(n :: Int) -> String do
  if n > 0 do
    "positive"
  else if n < 0 do
    "negative"
  else
    "zero"
  end
end

fn main() do
  println(sign(-1))
end

codes.name: pass-through-arm
codes.title: match arm returning what it matched
codes.summary: A `case` arm's value is its own pattern written again, as in `Ok(n) -> Ok(n)`, which the pattern alone already means.
codes.repair: Delete the `->` and the value, and leave the pattern on its own as the arm: `Ok(n)`.

example.bad:
fn check(r) do
  case r do
    Ok(n) -> Ok(n)
    Err(e) -> Err("check failed: #{e}")
  end
end

fn main() do
  let _r = check(Err("no input"))
end
example.fixed:
fn check(r) do
  case r do
    Ok(n)
    Err(e) -> Err("check failed: #{e}")
  end
end

fn main() do
  let _r = check(Err("no input"))
end

codes.name: bool-comparison
codes.title: comparison with a Bool literal
codes.summary: A value is compared with `true` or `false` using `==` or `!=`, which is the value itself or its negation.
codes.repair: Write the value alone in place of `== true` or `!= false`, and `not` the value in place of `== false` or `!= true`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let ready = true
  if ready == true do
    println("ready")
  end
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let ready = true
  if ready do
    println("ready")
  end
end

codes.name: manifest-unreadable
codes.title: cannot read package manifest
codes.summary: The project manifest could not be opened or read as UTF-8.
codes.repair: Create mesh.toml in the project directory or restore read access to it.

codes.name: manifest-invalid
codes.title: invalid package manifest
codes.summary: The manifest contains invalid TOML or violates the package schema.
codes.repair: Correct the indicated field in mesh.toml. Include a [package] table with string name and version fields.

codes.name: entrypoint-not-found
codes.title: entrypoint not found
codes.summary: The project does not contain the expected Mesh entrypoint file.
codes.repair: Set [package].entrypoint to an existing project-relative .mpl file or remove it and create main.mpl.

codes.name: lockfile-invalid
codes.title: cannot use dependency lockfile
codes.summary: The mesh.lock file could not be read, parsed, or written.
codes.repair: Fix the indicated TOML or restore access to mesh.lock, then rerun the dependency command.

codes.name: dependency-unresolvable
codes.title: cannot resolve dependency
codes.summary: A dependency could not be located, fetched, or checked out.
codes.repair: Correct the dependency path or Git source in mesh.toml and run meshc deps, or run meshpkg install for a registry dependency.

codes.name: dependency-cycle
codes.title: dependency cycle
codes.summary: The package dependency chain returns to a package it already visits.
codes.repair: Remove a dependency from the cycle or move shared code into a package both sides can depend on.

codes.name: dependency-conflict
codes.title: conflicting dependency sources
codes.summary: The same dependency name is required from different sources.
codes.repair: Update the dependency declarations to use a single source for that name.

codes.name: module-cycle
codes.title: module import cycle
codes.summary: The import chain returns to a module it already visits.
codes.repair: Remove an import from the cycle or move shared definitions to a separate module.

codes.name: module-unreadable
codes.title: cannot load project module
codes.summary: A module could not be read or assigned an unambiguous name inside the project.
codes.repair: Check the module path and its read permissions. Use a uniquely named .mpl file inside the project with no symbolic links.

codes.name: native-binding-invalid
codes.title: invalid native binding
codes.summary: A manifest-declared native binding could not be loaded as a package file.
codes.repair: Set [native].bindings to package-relative paths to regular .mpl files outside the test tree.

codes.name: native-declaration-outside-binding
codes.title: native declaration outside a binding file
codes.summary: A native declaration occurs in a module that is not listed as a native binding.
codes.repair: Move the declaration into a file listed in [native].bindings or add its file to that list and provide the native archive.

codes.name: native-archive-missing
codes.title: native archive missing or invalid
codes.summary: The requested target has no readable, checksum-verified static archive in the native package.
codes.repair: Provide the static archive for the requested target and record its package-relative path and SHA-256 in [[native.libraries]].

codes.name: unexpected-token
codes.title: unexpected token
codes.summary: The parser reached a token the grammar does not allow at this point.
codes.repair: Remove the token, or replace it with what the label says the grammar expects here.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let = 1
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let _x = 1
end

codes.name: expected-token
codes.title: expected token missing
codes.summary: The grammar requires one particular token here, such as `do`, `->`, `in`, or a name, and the source has another one.
codes.repair: Write the token the message expects where the label points, or replace the token found there with it.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  for x [1, 2] do
    println("#{x}")
  end
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  for x in [1, 2] do
    println("#{x}")
  end
end

codes.name: unclosed-delimiter
codes.title: unclosed delimiter
codes.summary: A `(`, `[`, `{`, or string interpolation is still open where its contents end.
codes.repair: Add the matching `)`, `]`, or `}` where the contents end; the related span shows where the delimiter was opened. If the contents are a list, separate its items with `,`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  println("hi"
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  println("hi")
end

codes.name: missing-end
codes.title: missing `end`
codes.summary: A block opened with `do`, such as a function, `if`, `case`, loop, closure, or type body, has no `end` that closes it.
codes.repair: Add `end` where the block's body ends; the related span shows the `do` it closes. Each `do` takes its own `end`, so count them in nested blocks.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  println("hi")
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  println("hi")
end

codes.name: unknown-character
codes.title: unknown character
codes.summary: The source has a character that starts no Mesh token, such as `$`, `^`, or a backtick, outside a string or comment.
codes.repair: Delete the character, or move it into a string or a comment. For an operator, write one Mesh has, such as `*`, `&&`, or `<>`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let n = 2 ^ 3
  println("#{n}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let n = 2 * 3
  println("#{n}")
end

codes.name: unterminated-string
codes.title: unterminated string
codes.summary: A string literal has no closing quote, so it runs to the end of the file.
codes.repair: Add the closing `"` (`"""` for a triple-quoted string) where the text ends. Inside the string, write a quote as `\"`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  println("hello)
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  println("hello")
end

codes.name: unterminated-interpolation
codes.title: unterminated interpolation
codes.summary: A string interpolation opened with `#{` or `${` has no closing `}`, so it runs to the end of the file.
codes.repair: Close the interpolation with `}` after its expression, then close the string with `"`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let x = 1
  println("x is #{x
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let x = 1
  println("x is #{x}")
end

codes.name: unterminated-block-comment
codes.title: unterminated block comment
codes.summary: A block comment opened with `#=` has no closing `=#`, so it runs to the end of the file. Block comments nest: each `#=` inside one needs its own `=#`.
codes.repair: Add `=#` where the comment ends, one for each `#=` it contains.

example.bad:
#= Prints a greeting.
fn main() do
  println("hi")
end
example.fixed:
#= Prints a greeting. =#
fn main() do
  println("hi")
end

codes.name: invalid-slot-pipe
codes.title: invalid slot pipe
codes.summary: A pipe is written `|0>`, `|1>`, or `|N` without `>`. Slot pipes are numbered from 2, because `|>` already pipes into the first argument.
codes.repair: Write `|>` to pipe into the first argument, or `|N>` with N from 2 up to pipe into argument N.

example.bad:
fn add(a :: Int, b :: Int) -> Int = a + b

fn main() do
  let n = 1 |1> add(2)
  println("#{n}")
end
example.fixed:
fn add(a :: Int, b :: Int) -> Int = a + b

fn main() do
  let n = 1 |> add(2)
  println("#{n}")
end

codes.name: invalid-regex-literal
codes.title: invalid regex literal
codes.summary: A `~` does not start a well-formed regex literal `~r/pattern/flags`: the `r/` is missing, the pattern has no closing `/`, or a flag is not `i`, `m`, or `s`.
codes.repair: Write the literal as `~r/pattern/flags`: escape a `/` in the pattern as `\/`, end the pattern with `/`, and use only the flags `i`, `m`, and `s`.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let rx = ~r/[a-z]+/x
  println("#{Regex.is_match(rx, "abc")}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let rx = ~r/[a-z]+/i
  println("#{Regex.is_match(rx, "abc")}")
end

codes.name: single-ampersand
codes.title: single `&`
codes.summary: A lone `&` stands where an operator is expected. Mesh has no `&` operator: logical and is `&&` or `and`.
codes.repair: Write `&&` or `and` for a logical and.

example.bad:
fn main() do
  let ok = true & false
  println("#{ok}")
end
example.fixed:
fn main() do
  let ok = true && false
  println("#{ok}")
end

codes.name: law-syntax
codes.title: law file syntax error
codes.summary: A `.law` file does not follow the law grammar: `from Module import name` lines, then `law` declarations written like functions, then `proof` blocks.
codes.repair: Write target imports first, then `law name(param :: Type, ...) -> Type do ... end` for each imported function, then `proof name do ... end` with `refl`, `exact`, `congr`, `induction`, or `cases`, one entry per line.

codes.name: law-too-large
codes.title: law file nested too deeply
codes.summary: A law body or proof in a `.law` file nests deeper than the law parser accepts.
codes.repair: Flatten the deepest part: move a nested expression into a helper function of the module under test, or split a deep proof into lemmas used with `exact`.

codes.name: logic-syntax
codes.title: logic syntax error
codes.summary: A `logic do ... end` block or a `.law` file starting with `logic` does not follow the logic grammar of `from` imports, then `inductive`, `fn`, `theorem`, and `proof` declarations.
codes.repair: Write the token the message expects where the label points: separate entries with new lines or `;`, close each `do` with `end`, write equality as `==`, and annotate binders as `name :: Type`.

example.bad:
logic do
  theorem two() do 2 = 2 end
end

fn main() do
end
example.fixed:
logic do
  theorem two() do 2 == 2 end
end

fn main() do
end

codes.name: logic-too-large
codes.title: logic source too large
codes.summary: A logic block or file nests terms or proofs deeper than the logic parser accepts, or is larger than 4 GiB.
codes.repair: Name the deepest subterm with `let` or a separate `fn` declaration, split a deep proof into lemmas used with `exact`, or split the file.

codes.name: test-file-syntax
codes.title: test file structure error
codes.summary: A `describe` block in a `.test.mpl` file has its `setup` after one of its tests, or more than one `teardown`.
codes.repair: Put a describe's `setup` before its first `test` or nested `describe`, and merge its teardowns into one `teardown do ... end`.

codes.name: panic
codes.title: runtime panic
codes.summary: The program panicked while it ran: it called `panic(...)`, or hit a runtime error such as `List.get` past the end, `Map.get` of a missing key, a value no match arm or function clause accepts, or an integer division by zero. The panic ends the actor it ran in, or the program with exit status 101 when it ran in `main`.
codes.repair: Handle the case the message names before the operation runs: check an index against `List.length`, a key with `Map.has_key`, a divisor against zero, or add the missing match arm. Return a `Result` instead of calling `panic` for a failure the caller should handle, and supervise an actor that may still fail so it restarts.

codes.name: stack-overflow
codes.title: stack overflow
codes.summary: A function recursed deeper than the stack of the program or actor it ran in allows, and the runtime aborted the whole process.
codes.repair: Make the recursion a direct self-call in tail position, which runs as a loop in constant stack, often by carrying the result in an accumulator parameter; or rewrite it with `List.reduce` or another iterator.

codes.name: actor-crashed
codes.title: actor crashed in the runtime
codes.summary: An actor ended with a failure that is not a Mesh panic: the runtime, or native code the actor called, failed while it ran. Linked actors and the actor's supervisor receive its exit as they would a panic's.
codes.repair: Read the runtime's report above this diagnostic. Report it with the program that reproduces it; until it is fixed, avoid the call the report names, and supervise the actor so a supervisor restarts it.

codes.name: supervisor-gave-up
codes.title: supervisor gave up
codes.summary: A supervisor's children failed more often than its `max_restarts` within `max_seconds` allow, so it stopped all of its children and exited instead of restarting them again.
codes.repair: Fix the failure that makes the child crash on start or soon after, which the runtime reports before this diagnostic. Raise `max_restarts` or `max_seconds` only if the failures are expected and transient.

codes.name: library-invalid-argument
codes.title: invalid library call argument
codes.summary: A host called the library with a `NULL` response pointer, a `NULL` request with a non-zero length, or a `NULL` callback table; the call returned status 1 (`MESH_LIBRARY_ERR_INVALID_ARGUMENT`).
codes.repair: Pass a pointer to a zero-initialized `MeshLibraryBytes` for the response, a request pointer whenever its length is not zero, and a callback table built from the generated header.

codes.name: library-not-initialized
codes.title: library not initialized
codes.summary: A host called the library before `mesh_library_init`, or after `mesh_library_shutdown`; the call returned status 2 (`MESH_LIBRARY_ERR_NOT_INITIALIZED`).
codes.repair: Call `mesh_library_init` once, check that it returns 0, then make the other calls. A library cannot be started again in the same process after `mesh_library_shutdown`, so shut it down only as the process ends.

codes.name: library-busy
codes.title: library call already in progress
codes.summary: A host called an exported function while another exported call was running in the same process; the library runs one call at a time, and this one returned status 3 (`MESH_LIBRARY_ERR_BUSY`).
codes.repair: Make the calls one at a time, from one serial queue or behind a lock, or retry the call after the one in progress returns.

codes.name: library-panic
codes.title: exported function panicked
codes.summary: The exported Mesh function panicked; the runtime reported the panic on standard error, and the call returned status 4 (`MESH_LIBRARY_ERR_PANIC`) with an empty response.
codes.repair: Fix the panic the runtime reported (an `R0001`), or return an `Err` from the exported function for a failure the host should handle.

codes.name: library-host-callback-failed
codes.title: host callback status reserved
codes.summary: Status 5 (`MESH_LIBRARY_ERR_HOST_CALLBACK`) is reserved in library ABI 1 and no runtime function returns it: a failing host callback reaches Mesh code as `Err("host_callback_failed:<capability>:<status>")` instead.
codes.repair: Check that the host was built against the header generated with the library it links. To learn why a host callback failed, handle the `Err` the Mesh code receives from it.

codes.name: library-output-too-large
codes.title: library payload too large
codes.summary: A request or a result crossing the library boundary was larger than 1 MiB, or the host's allocator could not allocate the response; the call returned status 6 (`MESH_LIBRARY_ERR_OUTPUT_TOO_LARGE`).
codes.repair: Keep each request and result under 1 MiB: split a large payload across several calls, or pass a reference such as a key or a path instead of the data.

codes.name: library-abi-mismatch
codes.title: library ABI mismatch
codes.summary: The host's callback table has an `abi_version` other than the runtime's (1), or a `struct_size` other than the size of `MeshLibraryHostCallbacksV1`; registration returned status 7 (`MESH_LIBRARY_ERR_ABI`).
codes.repair: Build the callback table from the header generated with the library: set `abi_version` to `MESH_LIBRARY_ABI_VERSION` and `struct_size` to `sizeof(MeshLibraryHostCallbacksV1)`, and rebuild the host after regenerating the library.

codes.name: library-callback-missing
codes.title: host callback missing
codes.summary: Mesh code used a host capability, such as the secure store, with no callback registered for it; it receives `Err("host_callback_missing")`, and status 8 (`MESH_LIBRARY_ERR_CALLBACK_MISSING`) is reserved for the host side.
codes.repair: Register a callback for the capability with `mesh_library_register_host_callbacks` after `mesh_library_init`, or handle the `Err` in the Mesh code that uses it.

codes.name: library-application-error
codes.title: exported function returned an error
codes.summary: The exported Mesh function returned `Err`; the call returned status 9 (`MESH_LIBRARY_ERR_APPLICATION`) and the response holds the error's message.
codes.repair: Handle the message in the host as the function's error result, or change the input so the function returns `Ok`.

codes.name: node-connect-failed
codes.title: node connection failed
codes.summary: `Node.connect` could not reach or authenticate the remote node, or this node was never started.
codes.repair: Start this node with `Node.start(name, cookie)` before connecting, give `Node.connect` the peer's `name@host:port` with the peer listening there, and start both nodes with the same cookie.

codes.name: assert-failed
codes.title: `assert` failed
codes.summary: The condition of an `assert` was false, which ends and fails its test.
codes.repair: Fix the code under test so the condition holds, or correct the condition if it states the wrong expectation; the message shows it as written.

codes.name: assert-eq-failed
codes.title: `assert_eq` sides differ
codes.summary: The two sides of an `assert_eq` show different text, compared as `"#{value}"` shows them, which ends and fails its test.
codes.repair: Compare the `left` and `right` values in the message, and fix the code under test or the expected value, whichever is wrong.

codes.name: assert-ne-failed
codes.title: `assert_ne` sides are equal
codes.summary: The two sides of an `assert_ne` show the same text, which ends and fails its test.
codes.repair: Fix the code under test so the values differ, or correct the assertion if they are meant to be equal.

codes.name: assert-raises-failed
codes.title: `assert_raises` did not raise
codes.summary: The function given to `assert_raises` returned without panicking or failing an assertion.
codes.repair: Make the function perform the operation that should fail, such as `List.get` past the end or a `panic(...)`, or drop the `assert_raises` if the operation is meant to succeed.

codes.name: assert-receive-failed
codes.title: `assert_receive` got no matching message
codes.summary: No message arrived before the `assert_receive` timeout (100 ms unless given), or the first message to arrive did not match its pattern.
